domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: A patient aspirates gastric contents intraoperatively and subsequently becomes hypoxic. What is the mainstay of therapy?
answer: Positive-pressure ventilation (PPV); may require intubation + PEEP or noninvasive ventilation
rationale: Aspiration-induced chemical pneumonitis impairs gas exchange; PPV recruits atelectatic alveoli and corrects hypoxemia.
confusable_with: antibiotics (not indicated empirically unless culture-positive)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: After confirmed particulate aspiration, which additional procedure is indicated beyond PPV?
answer: Bronchoscopy and pulmonary lavage for particulate removal
rationale: Particulate matter causes mechanical obstruction and ongoing inflammation; bronchoscopic lavage removes debris that PPV alone cannot clear.
confusable_with: corticosteroids (not recommended after aspiration)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What two gastric parameters define the threshold at which a patient is at high risk for aspiration pneumonitis?
answer: Gastric volume >25 mL (0.4 mL/kg) AND gastric pH <2.5
rationale: Large volumes of acidic gastric contents cause severe chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) when aspirated.
confusable_with: volume alone (both volume AND pH thresholds must be met)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: All obstetric patients are treated as having a full stomach. What anesthetic implication follows?
answer: Prefer regional anesthesia; if general required, use RSI with cricoid pressure until ETT confirmed
rationale: Progesterone-mediated lower esophageal sphincter relaxation and delayed gastric emptying elevate aspiration risk throughout pregnancy.
confusable_with: standard induction (inappropriate without RSI precautions in full-stomach patients)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What does evidence show regarding routine metoclopramide, H2-blockers, or PPIs for aspiration prevention in elective cases?
answer: No evidence supports routine use in elective cases; reserved for high-risk patients
rationale: ASA guidelines confirm no morbidity/mortality benefit from routine pharmacologic aspiration prophylaxis in healthy patients undergoing elective procedures.
confusable_with: mandatory H2-blocker use (guideline-discordant for routine elective cases)

domain: Airway management (assessment & prediction, supraglottic & ETT devices, laryngoscopy/video, awake intubation, difficult & failed airway algorithm, extubation, complications)
stem: What is the recommended maximum bag-mask ventilation pressure to minimize gastric insufflation?
answer: Less than 20 cmH2O
rationale: Mask pressures exceeding 20 cmH2O overcome the lower esophageal sphincter and force gas into the stomach, increasing regurgitation and aspiration risk.
confusable_with: 30 cmH2O (the plateau pressure limit for lung protection, not mask ventilation)

enabling_conditions: Full stomach (obstetric, emergency, gastroparesis, bowel obstruction), reduced consciousness, difficult airway
pathophysiology: Gastric acid (pH<2.5) causes chemical pneumonitis; particles cause mechanical obstruction; both trigger inflammatory cascade and alveolar-capillary leak
time_course: Immediate bronchospasm and laryngospasm; ARDS-like picture 2-6 hours later
key_features: Wheezing, hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates on CXR; may be clinically silent at the time of aspiration event
consequence_if_missed: Progressive ARDS, respiratory failure, death; significant fraction of anesthesia-related maternal mortality

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: What are the three main ANCA-associated vasculitides classified at the 2012 Chapel Hill Consensus Conference?
answer: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)
rationale: These three small-vessel vasculitides share ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation and form the AAV group.
confusable_with: polyarteritis nodosa (medium-vessel, ANCA-negative)

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: In microscopic polyangiitis, which ANCA target antigen is most commonly positive, and in what percentage?
answer: Anti-MPO (myeloperoxidase) in approximately 70% of MPA patients
rationale: MPO is the primary autoantigen in MPA; anti-PR3 accounts for ~20% and 10% are ANCA-negative.
confusable_with: anti-PR3 (predominant in GPA, not MPA)

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: ANCA serology is essential but not sufficient for AAV diagnosis. What other conditions produce positive ANCA?
answer: SLE, Goodpasture syndrome, infective endocarditis, chronic hepatitis
rationale: ANCA positivity is neither 100% sensitive nor specific; clinical, laboratory, and histologic correlation is required for definitive AAV diagnosis.
confusable_with: ANCA as a stand-alone diagnostic test (guideline-discordant)

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: What is double-positive antibody disease and how does it influence management?
answer: Concurrent ANCA + anti-GBM antibodies; renal manifestations follow anti-GBM pattern, systemic features follow AAV pattern, requiring treatment addressing both
rationale: 10-50% of anti-GBM patients have detectable ANCA (usually anti-MPO); positive ANCA is thought to precede anti-GBM by exposing GBM epitopes.
confusable_with: pure Goodpasture syndrome (lacks systemic ANCA-vasculitis features)

domain: Internal medicine: rheumatology, immunology & allergy (gout & crystal arthropathy, SLE, RA, vasculitides, anaphylaxis & angioedema, drug reactions)
stem: What drug class is a recognized cause of ANCA-positive drug-induced vasculitis?
answer: Anti-TNF-alpha therapy (for RA, ankylosing spondylitis)
rationale: Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis can be triggered by anti-TNF agents; cessation of the offending drug is part of management.
confusable_with: primary AAV (drug-induced form remits with drug cessation)

discriminator: GPA: anti-PR3/c-ANCA, granulomatous inflammation, upper respiratory tract + kidney; MPA: anti-MPO/p-ANCA, non-granulomatous, kidney + lung without upper-tract involvement

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What is the Berlin definition severity classification of ARDS by PaO2/FiO2 ratio?
answer: Mild: PaO2/FiO2 <=300; Moderate: <=200; Severe: <=100 mmHg
rationale: The 2012 Berlin definition stratifies ARDS by P/F ratio to guide prognosis and ventilator management.
confusable_with: cardiogenic pulmonary edema (elevated PAOP, responds to diuresis; ARDS is non-cardiogenic)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: Which single intervention has shown the greatest mortality benefit in ARDS?
answer: Reduced tidal volumes (lung-protective ventilation, 6 mL/kg ideal body weight)
rationale: The ARDSNet trial demonstrated that limiting Vt reduces volutrauma and barotrauma, producing the largest survival benefit of any ARDS intervention tested in RCTs.
confusable_with: corticosteroids (no consistent mortality benefit in ARDS)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What two mechanisms produce pulmonary edema, and which underlies ARDS?
answer: Hydrostatic (cardiogenic) vs. increased alveolar-capillary permeability (non-cardiogenic); ARDS is permeability edema
rationale: In ARDS, cytokine-mediated alveolar-capillary barrier disruption floods alveoli with protein-rich fluid independent of hydrostatic pressure.
confusable_with: cardiogenic pulmonary edema (hydrostatic, responds to preload reduction)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: What plateau pressure limit is a key tenet of lung-protective ventilation in ARDS?
answer: Plateau pressure <30 cmH2O
rationale: Limiting plateau pressure reduces barotrauma; combined with low Vt (6 mL/kg IBW) and higher PEEP, this prevents ventilator-induced lung injury.
confusable_with: peak inspiratory pressure (plateau is end-inspiratory pause pressure, the true alveolar distension measure)

domain: ICU Critical Care
stem: Prolonged FiO2 >50-60% causes pulmonary toxicity via what mechanism?
answer: Intracellular free radical generation (superoxide, hydroxyl ions, hydrogen peroxide) damaging alveolar epithelium
rationale: High O2 tensions generate reactive oxygen species that are cytotoxic to lung cells, worsening the injury being treated.
confusable_with: 100% O2 always harmful (short-term 100% O2 up to 10-20 hours is generally safe)

enabling_conditions: Sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, trauma, pancreatitis, transfusion (TRALI)
pathophysiology: Diffuse alveolar damage from cytokine-mediated alveolar-capillary permeability increase; protein-rich exudate floods alveoli; reduced surfactant; hyaline membranes
time_course: Acute onset within 1 week of known clinical insult; bilateral infiltrates on CXR; not fully explained by cardiac failure
key_features: Hypoxia (P/F <=300), bilateral CXR infiltrates, absent cardiogenic cause, requires positive pressure ventilation
consequence_if_missed: Progressive hypoxic respiratory failure, multi-organ failure, death; severe ARDS mortality 30-40%

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: A ventilated patient develops rising peak airway pressure simultaneous with rising PEEP and arterial hypotension. What must be excluded immediately?
answer: Tension pneumothorax
rationale: High intrathoracic pressure from tension pneumothorax impedes venous return causing hypotension; concurrent rise in both peak and plateau pressures indicates decreased compliance from pneumothorax.
confusable_with: bronchospasm (raises peak but not plateau; no hemodynamic collapse)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Increased peak inspiratory pressure with normal plateau pressure during mechanical ventilation indicates what problem?
answer: Increased airway resistance (bronchospasm, ETT obstruction/kinking, secretions) — not a compliance problem
rationale: Plateau pressure reflects alveolar/parenchymal compliance; if only peak rises (not plateau), the problem is in the conducting airway.
confusable_with: decreased lung compliance (raises both peak AND plateau)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: What are the three forms of ventilator-induced lung injury that lung-protective ventilation aims to prevent?
answer: Barotrauma (pressure-mediated), volutrauma (volume-mediated), atelectrauma (cyclic recruitment-derecruitment)
rationale: Low Vt limits volutrauma; plateau pressure limit reduces barotrauma; adequate PEEP prevents atelectrauma from repeated alveolar collapse.
confusable_with: biotrauma (cytokine-mediated systemic injury — a fourth mechanism)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In a surgical patient with active ARDS, what should guide intraoperative ventilation strategy?
answer: Continue lung-protective ventilation: Vt 4-6 mL/kg IBW, PEEP, limit plateau pressure; permissive hypercapnia acceptable
rationale: Anesthetic management of critically ill patients with acute pulmonary disorders should continue intensive care principles intraoperatively to avoid worsening VILI.
confusable_with: standard 8-10 mL/kg Vt (harmful in ARDS due to volutrauma)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: What preoperative aspiration precautions should be taken for high-risk patients to reduce ARDS from aspiration?
answer: Metoclopramide + H2-blocker + antacid preop; awake or upright intubation or RSI; NGT to suction if present
rationale: High-risk patients require pharmacologic and procedural strategies to reduce gastric volume and acidity, preventing the aspiration that precipitates chemical pneumonitis and ARDS.
confusable_with: routine elective patients (no evidence for pharmacologic prophylaxis in low-risk patients)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What is the goal of damage control surgery (DCS) for abdominal trauma?
answer: Stop hemorrhage and limit GI contamination; defer definitive repair until patient is physiologically stabilized
rationale: DCS prioritizes life-threatening bleeding control and GI contamination containment over anatomic repair, allowing resuscitation and physiologic normalization before definitive surgery.
confusable_with: definitive repair (this is deferred until patient is more stable; hollow viscus disconnected, not repaired)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What vascular structures are primarily at risk in pelvic ring fractures causing life-threatening hemorrhage?
answer: Superior gluteal artery (branches from internal iliac) plus inferior gluteal, rectal, obturator, and vesical arteries; venous injury common alongside arterial
rationale: Pelvic ring fractures disrupt intrapelvic vasculature; hemorrhage from these vessels can fill the pelvic retroperitoneum rapidly and is a major cause of trauma mortality.
confusable_with: external iliac artery (less commonly injured in pelvic ring fractures)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What does a FAST exam detect in pelvic trauma, and what is its limitation?
answer: Detects free fluid; cannot differentiate bowel contents from blood
rationale: FAST is rapid bedside ultrasound identifying free peritoneal fluid, but it lacks specificity to distinguish hemorrhage from GI spillage, limiting diagnostic certainty.
confusable_with: CT scan (differentiates fluid types and identifies organ injuries; requires hemodynamic stability)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: What monitoring tools guide targeted blood product resuscitation in pelvic trauma?
answer: TEG (thromboelastography) or ROTEM (rotational thromboelastometry)
rationale: Viscoelastic assays provide real-time assessment of the entire coagulation process, enabling goal-directed transfusion of specific blood components rather than empiric 1:1:1 ratios.
confusable_with: standard coagulation panel (PT/aPTT/fibrinogen — slower, less actionable in acute hemorrhage)

domain: Internal medicine: emergency & acute care (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, trauma primary survey, toxicology & overdoses, environmental emergencies, anaphylaxis, acute abdomen)
stem: In a hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected pelvic fracture, what quick imaging study directs care without delaying resuscitation?
answer: Pelvic X-ray (rapid, can identify pelvic ring disruption and guide intervention without CT)
rationale: In unstable patients, a quick AP pelvic X-ray can identify life-threatening pelvic ring fractures and direct hemorrhage control (binder, IR, DCS) without the time delay of CT.
confusable_with: CT scan (requires hemodynamic stability; inappropriate if patient too unstable to leave trauma bay)

enabling_conditions: High-energy trauma (MVA, falls, crush); pelvic ring fractures; blunt or penetrating abdominal injury
pathophysiology: Disruption of pelvic vasculature (particularly internal iliac branches) leads to retroperitoneal hematoma and hemorrhagic shock; hollow viscus injury causes peritoneal contamination
time_course: Immediate hemorrhagic shock; peritonitis may develop over hours after viscus injury
key_features: Hemodynamic instability, pelvic tenderness, free fluid on FAST, pelvic ring disruption on X-ray
consequence_if_missed: Exsanguination from uncontrolled pelvic hemorrhage; delayed peritonitis from missed hollow viscus injury
